cells.tense: You are handing over something finished, and you know what it cost to make.
cells.ask: Offer one thing you made — a meal, a plan, a repair — and when someone moves to give back, let them. Don't wave it off, don't match it in the same breath. Take the return and let the thing be even.
cells.core:
You're at the end of making something, and it finishes where it meets another person. Not the second you stop working — the second it lands with someone and they take it in. You know what went into it, and you're still in the room while they weigh it.

What gets in the way is the extra step. You hand something over, then hand over more to make the first one comfortable — topping it up, sending back whatever comes, keeping one hand on it after it leaves. Open hands that are also braced. The staying power you need now sits in the receiving. Letting something be paid for is its own kind of strength.
cells.sheetLine: You made it, you handed it over, and you're letting them take it in.
cells.verb: offering what you made for what you need, and taking what is offered
cells.place: the moment a finished thing leaves your hands

cells.tense: You're already paying for things tomorrow, and no one has held out a hand yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you were about to give, and don't give it yet. Wait until someone actually asks or offers. Let the day pass with it ungiven.
cells.core:
A hand goes out and a hand comes back at about the same pace. You offer, they take, something returns, and neither person holds the whole thing up alone. There's a bottom to what you put in and a bottom to what comes back.

What's happening instead is that you've moved the exchange ahead of the clock. Someone might need something, so you've already decided what you'll hand over, already felt the cost, already written how they'll answer. You're holding out things nobody reached for. There's an edge of bracing to it — not free, but fortified against a future where you come up short. What's needed here is strength that holds still rather than reaches. A shoulder that bears weight without grabbing the load. Let the other hand open first.

cells.tense: You stopped putting things into the shared stream a while back, and you can still see the spot.
cells.ask: Take one small skill you have — measuring, listening, fixing — and use it on something that isn't yours. Your neighbor's gate, a friend's essay, the office plant.
cells.core:
You're holding what you made close, and not much is moving between you and anyone. You know the give-and-take is supposed to work, but you're standing off the road watching traffic go by without you in it. This is where something gets finished and let out into the open — yours is closing inward.

The muscle that's gone is attention. You can still notice what's fair and what isn't, you're just not aiming that noticing at anything shared. Practice that stays home sharpens you and walls you in at the same time. Point the eye at something outside your own head and handing things over starts to feel less like risk and more like ordinary traffic.

cells.tense: You're already keeping the exchange even on both sides, and you file it under being reasonable.
cells.ask: Catch yourself doing one thing that keeps an exchange even — waiting your turn, paying back, splitting the check — and say out loud, at least to yourself, 'I did that on purpose.'
cells.core:
There's a fairness running through how you handle what sits between you and other people. You notice when someone's shorted, you adjust without announcing it, you hand back what came to you. That's reciprocal, and it isn't automatic — it's you doing it. You'd call it practical. Just being reasonable. The accounting gets done and gets filed under nothing special.

That's the part that belongs to you and hasn't been claimed. The steady back-and-forth isn't a background condition of life; it's something you're running. No need to announce it to the people around you. The work is to stop letting it count as background.
